title: Unnecessary length in the Executive Document is treated as a defect, because disclosure that goes unread has no legitimacy value
content:
A.1.10.2.4.8.1.3 states the trade-off outright: "While transparency and access to information are essential, the document should avoid unnecessary length or complexity." The best practices that follow are all length-reducing — "use strategic hyperlinks and text formatting to reduce the document's length while maintaining accessibility," "regularly review and update templates to eliminate unnecessary content," and present information in priority order.

The justification is behavioural: "A concise and well-structured document increases the likelihood that voters will read, understand, and consider the actions on which they are voting."

This is a rejection of the maximal-disclosure instinct that governs most governance writing, where adding detail is always defensible and nobody is ever blamed for including too much. The Atlas treats padding as harmful, because a document that is technically complete but unread produces uninformed votes with a clean paper trail — which fails the standard set at A.1.10.2.4.8.1.1 while appearing to satisfy it.

Hyperlinking is what makes the trade-off non-destructive: depth is relocated rather than removed, so the document stays short for the median reader while remaining exhaustive for anyone who follows the links. The residual risk is that link targets are not covered by the same review discipline as the document, so completeness now depends on the durability and accuracy of what sits one hop away.
description: A.1.10.2.4.8.1.3 puts transparency and comprehension in explicit tension and resolves it with hyperlinking — depth moves off the page rather than being deleted.
